chapters.title: Introduction to Data Structures
chapters.description: Understanding data structures, their importance, and complexity analysis

pages.title: What is a Data Structure?
pages.content: A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently. Data structures help in managing large amounts of data and allow programs to perform operations like searching, sorting, and updating efficiently.
keyPoints: Data structures organize and store data
Examples include arrays, stacks, queues, and trees
Used in almost every software application

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a data structure?
options: To organize and store data efficiently
quiz.explanation: Data structures organize and store data efficiently for processing.

pages.title: Types of Data Structures
pages.content: Data structures are mainly classified into two categories: linear and non-linear data structures. Linear structures arrange elements sequentially, while non-linear structures arrange data hierarchically.
pages.exampleCode:
// Linear structure example
int arr[3] = {10,20,30};
keyPoints: Linear data structures store elements sequentially
Examples: Array, Stack, Queue, Linked List
Non-linear data structures organize data hierarchically

quiz.question: Which of the following is a linear data structure?
quiz.explanation: Arrays store elements sequentially, making them a linear data structure.

pages.title: Importance of Data Structures
pages.content: Data structures play a key role in writing efficient algorithms. They help in optimizing time and memory usage. Many real-world systems such as search engines, databases, and operating systems rely heavily on efficient data structures.
keyPoints: Used in databases and operating systems

quiz.question: Why are data structures important?
quiz.explanation: Data structures improve efficiency, reduce complexity, and organize data.

pages.title: Time Complexity
pages.content: Time complexity measures how the execution time of an algorithm grows as the input size increases. It helps programmers understand how efficient an algorithm is.
keyPoints: Common notations include O(n), O(log n)

quiz.question: What does time complexity measure?
options: Execution time relative to input size
quiz.explanation: Time complexity measures how execution time grows with input size.

pages.title: Space Complexity
pages.content: Space complexity measures the amount of memory an algorithm uses during execution. Efficient algorithms aim to minimize both time and space complexity.
pages.exampleCode:
// Example using extra memory
int arr[n];
keyPoints: Includes input memory and auxiliary memory

quiz.question: What does space complexity measure?
quiz.explanation: Space complexity measures how much memory an algorithm uses.

pages.title: Big-O Notation
pages.content: Big-O notation describes the performance of an algorithm in terms of time or space complexity. It represents the worst-case scenario of an algorithm's growth rate.
pages.exampleCode:
// Constant time example
int x = arr[0];
keyPoints: Common examples: O(1), O(n), O(log n)

quiz.question: Which notation describes algorithm complexity?
quiz.explanation: Big-O notation describes the complexity of algorithms.

chapters.title: C++ Basics for DSA
chapters.description: Understanding basic C++ concepts required for learning Data Structures and Algorithms

pages.title: Introduction to C++ for DSA
pages.content: C++ is one of the most widely used programming languages for learning Data Structures and Algorithms. It provides powerful features like pointers, memory control, and fast execution which are essential for competitive programming and system development.
keyPoints: C++ is widely used for competitive programming
Fast execution compared to many languages

quiz.question: Why is C++ commonly used for DSA?
options: Because it provides memory control and speed
Because it only works on Windows
quiz.explanation: C++ provides direct memory management and fast execution which makes it ideal for DSA.

pages.title: Variables and Data Types
pages.content: Variables are used to store data in programs. In C++, each variable must have a data type that determines what type of data it can store such as integers, characters, or floating point numbers.
keyPoints: Each variable has a data type
Common types include int, float, char, double

quiz.question: Which data type stores whole numbers in C++?
quiz.explanation: The int data type stores whole numbers.

pages.title: Input and Output (cin and cout)
pages.content: C++ uses the input stream 'cin' to receive input from the user and 'cout' to display output to the screen. These are part of the iostream library.

quiz.question: Which statement is used to take input in C++?
quiz.explanation: cin is used to take input from the user.

pages.title: Functions in C++
pages.content: Functions are blocks of code designed to perform specific tasks. They help organize programs and allow code reuse.
keyPoints: They divide large programs into smaller parts

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of using functions?
quiz.explanation: Functions allow code reuse and improve program structure.

pages.title: Arrays in C++
pages.content: Arrays store multiple values of the same data type in a single variable. They are widely used in DSA because many algorithms operate on arrays.
keyPoints: Elements must have same data type

quiz.question: What is the index of the first element in an array?
quiz.explanation: Array indexing starts from 0.

pages.title: Pointers in C++
pages.content: Pointers store the memory address of variables. They are powerful tools used in data structures like linked lists, trees, and graphs.

quiz.question: What does a pointer store?
quiz.explanation: Pointers store the memory address of a variable.

chapters.title: Arrays in Data Structures
chapters.description: Understanding arrays and their operations in Data Structures and Algorithms

pages.title: Introduction to Arrays
pages.content: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations. Arrays allow efficient access to elements using their index and are widely used in algorithms.
keyPoints: All elements have the same data type

quiz.question: How are array elements accessed?
quiz.explanation: Array elements are accessed using their index positions.

pages.title: Array Traversal
pages.content: Array traversal means visiting each element of the array exactly once to perform operations like printing or modifying values.
keyPoints: Useful for printing or processing elements

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of array traversal?
quiz.explanation: Traversal requires visiting each element once, so it is O(n).

pages.title: Insertion in Array
pages.content: Insertion in an array means adding a new element at a specific position. Elements after that position must be shifted to the right.
keyPoints: Position must be within array bounds

quiz.question: What must happen before inserting an element in the middle of an array?
quiz.explanation: Elements must shift right to create space for insertion.

pages.title: Deletion in Array
pages.content: Deletion removes an element from the array. Elements after the deleted position must shift left to fill the gap.

quiz.question: What happens after deleting an element from an array?
quiz.explanation: Elements shift left to fill the deleted element's position.

pages.title: Searching in Arrays
pages.content: Searching is the process of finding an element in the array. The simplest method is Linear Search which checks each element sequentially.

quiz.question: Which search method checks elements one by one?
quiz.explanation: Linear search checks each element sequentially.

pages.title: Advantages and Limitations of Arrays
pages.content: Arrays provide fast access to elements using indexes but have limitations such as fixed size and expensive insertion or deletion operations.

quiz.question: What is the main limitation of arrays?
quiz.explanation: Arrays have a fixed size which cannot be easily changed.

chapters.title: Searching Algorithms
chapters.description: Understanding searching techniques used to find elements efficiently in data structures

pages.title: Introduction to Searching
pages.content: Searching is the process of finding a specific element in a data structure. Efficient searching algorithms are important for improving the performance of programs when working with large datasets.
keyPoints: Two main types: Linear Search and Binary Search

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a searching algorithm?
options: To find an element in a data structure
quiz.explanation: Searching algorithms are used to locate a specific element within a data structure.

pages.title: Linear Search
pages.content: Linear Search is the simplest searching algorithm. It checks each element of the array sequentially until the desired element is found or the array ends.
keyPoints: Works on sorted and unsorted arrays

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of Linear Search?
quiz.explanation: Linear search may check every element, so its complexity is O(n).

pages.title: Binary Search
pages.content: Binary Search is an efficient searching algorithm that works on sorted arrays. It repeatedly divides the search range into halves until the target element is found.

quiz.question: Binary search works on which type of array?
quiz.explanation: Binary search requires the array to be sorted.

pages.title: Binary Search Example
pages.content: Binary search repeatedly divides the array into two halves. If the middle element is greater than the target, the search continues in the left half; otherwise it continues in the right half.
keyPoints: Middle element divides the search range

quiz.question: What is the advantage of Binary Search?
options: Reduces search space by half each step
quiz.explanation: Binary search halves the search space each iteration, making it efficient.

pages.title: Linear Search vs Binary Search
pages.content: Linear search checks each element sequentially while binary search repeatedly divides the search space. Binary search is much faster for large sorted datasets.
pages.exampleCode:
// Linear Search O(n)
// Binary Search O(log n)
keyPoints: Linear search works on any array
Binary search is faster for large datasets
Binary search reduces search time significantly

quiz.question: Which search algorithm is faster for large sorted arrays?
quiz.explanation: Binary search is faster because it reduces the search space by half.

pages.title: Applications of Searching Algorithms
pages.content: Searching algorithms are widely used in many applications such as databases, search engines, dictionaries, and file systems to quickly locate data.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: Searching user ID in database

quiz.question: Where are searching algorithms commonly used?
quiz.explanation: Searching algorithms are used in many real-world applications.

chapters.title: Sorting Algorithms
chapters.description: Understanding basic sorting techniques used to arrange data efficiently

pages.title: Introduction to Sorting
pages.content: Sorting is the process of arranging elements of a data structure in a specific order, usually ascending or descending. Sorting makes searching and data processing more efficient.
keyPoints: Common orders are ascending and descending

quiz.question: What is the purpose of sorting?
quiz.explanation: Sorting arranges data elements in a particular order.

pages.title: Bubble Sort
pages.content: Bubble Sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. Larger elements move to the end of the array in each iteration.
keyPoints: Simple but inefficient for large data

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort?
quiz.explanation: Bubble Sort has time complexity of O(n^2).

pages.title: Selection Sort
pages.content: Selection Sort repeatedly finds the smallest element from the unsorted portion and places it at the beginning of the sorted portion.

quiz.question: What does Selection Sort do in each iteration?
quiz.explanation: Selection sort finds the smallest element and places it at the correct position.

pages.title: Insertion Sort
pages.content: Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each element into its correct position.
keyPoints: Works well for nearly sorted arrays

quiz.question: Insertion Sort works best for which type of data?
quiz.explanation: Insertion Sort performs well for nearly sorted arrays.

pages.title: Comparison of Sorting Algorithms
pages.content: Different sorting algorithms have different time complexities and performance characteristics. Choosing the right sorting algorithm depends on dataset size and requirements.
keyPoints: Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sort have O(n^2)
Sorting choice depends on data size

quiz.question: Which complexity do basic sorting algorithms share?
quiz.explanation: Basic sorting algorithms usually have O(n^2) complexity.

pages.title: Applications of Sorting
pages.content: Sorting algorithms are widely used in applications such as database indexing, search optimization, and data analysis.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: sorting student marks

quiz.question: Where are sorting algorithms commonly used?
quiz.explanation: Sorting algorithms are used in many real-world applications.

chapters.title: Advanced Sorting Algorithms
chapters.description: Understanding efficient sorting algorithms used in real-world applications and coding interviews

pages.title: Introduction to Advanced Sorting
pages.content: Advanced sorting algorithms improve efficiency compared to basic sorting techniques like Bubble Sort and Selection Sort. These algorithms are designed to handle large datasets efficiently.
pages.exampleCode: // Advanced sorting algorithms improve efficiency
keyPoints: More efficient than basic sorting algorithms
Examples include Merge Sort and Quick Sort

quiz.question: Why are advanced sorting algorithms used?
quiz.explanation: Advanced sorting algorithms improve performance for large datasets.

pages.title: Merge Sort
pages.content: Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm. It divides the array into two halves, sorts each half recursively, and then merges the sorted halves.

quiz.question: What strategy does Merge Sort use?
quiz.explanation: Merge Sort uses the divide-and-conquer approach.

pages.title: Quick Sort
pages.content: Quick Sort is another divide-and-conquer algorithm. It selects a pivot element and partitions the array around the pivot so that smaller elements come before it and larger elements come after it.
keyPoints: Average time complexity O(n log n)

quiz.question: What element is used in Quick Sort for partitioning?
quiz.explanation: Quick Sort uses a pivot element to partition the array.

pages.title: Heap Sort
pages.content: Heap Sort uses a binary heap data structure. It first builds a max heap and repeatedly extracts the maximum element to place it at the end of the array.

quiz.question: Which data structure is used in Heap Sort?
quiz.explanation: Heap Sort uses a binary heap data structure.

pages.title: Time Complexity Comparison
pages.content: Different sorting algorithms have different performance characteristics. Advanced algorithms like Merge Sort, Quick Sort, and Heap Sort perform significantly better for large datasets.
keyPoints: Merge Sort complexity O(n log n)
Quick Sort average complexity O(n log n)
Heap Sort complexity O(n log n)

quiz.question: Which complexity is common for advanced sorting algorithms?
quiz.explanation: Most advanced sorting algorithms have O(n log n) complexity.

pages.title: When to Use Each Sorting Algorithm
pages.content: Choosing the right sorting algorithm depends on factors like dataset size, memory constraints, and whether the data is already partially sorted.
pages.exampleCode: // Choose algorithm based on dataset size and requirements
keyPoints: Merge Sort works well for large datasets
Quick Sort is fastest in practice
Heap Sort guarantees O(n log n)
Algorithm choice depends on problem requirements

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm is usually fastest in practice?
quiz.explanation: Quick Sort is generally the fastest sorting algorithm in practice.

chapters.title: Strings in Data Structures
chapters.description: Understanding string operations and algorithms used in data structures and coding interviews

pages.title: Introduction to Strings
pages.content: A string is a sequence of characters used to represent text. In C++, strings can be represented using character arrays or the string class from the standard library.
keyPoints: Represented as character arrays or string class

quiz.question: What does a string store?
quiz.explanation: Strings store characters that form text.

pages.title: String Traversal
pages.content: String traversal means accessing each character of the string sequentially. This is commonly done using loops.

quiz.question: What does string traversal mean?
quiz.explanation: Traversal means visiting each character of the string.

pages.title: String Reversal
pages.content: String reversal means reversing the order of characters in a string. This is a common interview question.

quiz.question: What does string reversal do?
quiz.explanation: String reversal changes the order of characters from end to start.

pages.title: Palindrome Check
pages.content: A palindrome is a string that reads the same forward and backward. Checking for palindromes is a common algorithm problem.
keyPoints: Palindrome reads same forward and backward

quiz.question: Which word is a palindrome?
quiz.explanation: Madam reads the same forward and backward.

pages.title: Character Frequency Count
pages.content: Frequency counting means determining how many times each character appears in a string. This is useful for many string processing tasks.

quiz.question: What does frequency counting do?
quiz.explanation: Frequency counting calculates how many times each character appears.

pages.title: Applications of String Algorithms
pages.content: String algorithms are widely used in search engines, text processing, compilers, and data analysis systems.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: searching word in text

quiz.question: Where are string algorithms commonly used?
quiz.explanation: String algorithms are used in many real-world applications.

chapters.title: Recursion
chapters.description: Understanding recursion and solving problems using recursive algorithms in C++

pages.title: Introduction to Recursion
pages.content: Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a problem. It breaks the problem into smaller subproblems until a base condition is reached.
keyPoints: Recursion is when a function calls itself
Used to solve problems in smaller steps
Common in algorithms and data structures
Requires a base condition to stop

quiz.question: What is recursion?
quiz.explanation: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself.

pages.title: Base Case in Recursion
pages.content: The base case is the condition that stops the recursive calls. Without a base case, recursion will continue infinitely and cause a stack overflow.

quiz.question: Why is the base case important in recursion?
quiz.explanation: The base case stops the recursion from running infinitely.

pages.title: Factorial Using Recursion
pages.content: Factorial is a common example used to demonstrate recursion. The factorial of n is calculated as n multiplied by factorial of (n-1).

quiz.question: What is factorial of 5?

pages.title: Fibonacci Using Recursion
pages.content: The Fibonacci sequence is another example of recursion where each number is the sum of the previous two numbers.
keyPoints: Each term depends on previous two terms

quiz.question: What are the first two Fibonacci numbers?
quiz.explanation: The Fibonacci sequence starts with 0 and 1.

pages.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Recursion
pages.content: Recursion can simplify complex problems but may use more memory due to function call stack usage.
pages.exampleCode: // Recursive vs Iterative approaches

quiz.question: What is a disadvantage of recursion?
quiz.explanation: Recursive calls consume stack memory.

pages.title: Applications of Recursion
pages.content: Recursion is widely used in algorithms like tree traversal, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and backtracking problems.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: tree traversal uses recursion
keyPoints: Used in tree and graph algorithms

quiz.question: Where is recursion commonly used?
quiz.explanation: Recursion is used in many algorithmic techniques.

chapters.title: Linked Lists
chapters.description: Understanding linked lists and their operations in Data Structures using C++

pages.title: Introduction to Linked Lists
pages.content: A Linked List is a linear data structure where elements are stored in nodes. Each node contains data and a pointer that points to the next node in the sequence.
keyPoints: Linked list stores elements in nodes
Each node has data and a pointer
Size can grow or shrink during execution

quiz.question: What does a node in a linked list contain?
quiz.explanation: Each node contains data and a pointer to the next node.

pages.title: Singly Linked List
pages.content: In a singly linked list, each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. The last node points to NULL indicating the end of the list.
keyPoints: Each node points to next node
Most basic type of linked list

quiz.question: What does the last node in a singly linked list point to?
quiz.explanation: The last node points to NULL indicating the end of the list.

pages.title: Insertion in Linked List
pages.content: Insertion adds a new node to the linked list. It can be done at the beginning, middle, or end of the list.
keyPoints: Insertion can occur at multiple positions
Time complexity O(1) for head insertion

quiz.question: Where can insertion occur in a linked list?
quiz.explanation: Insertion can happen at beginning, middle, or end.

pages.title: Deletion in Linked List
pages.content: Deletion removes a node from the linked list. The previous node pointer is updated to skip the deleted node.

quiz.question: What must be updated when deleting a node?
quiz.explanation: Pointers must be updated to skip the deleted node.

pages.title: Doubly Linked List
pages.content: A doubly linked list contains two pointers in each node: one pointing to the next node and another pointing to the previous node.

quiz.question: How many pointers does a node in a doubly linked list contain?
quiz.explanation: Doubly linked list nodes have two pointers.

pages.title: Circular Linked List
pages.content: In a circular linked list, the last node points back to the first node instead of NULL, forming a circular structure.
pages.exampleCode: // lastNode->next = head;
keyPoints: Last node connects to first node

quiz.question: What does the last node point to in a circular linked list?
quiz.explanation: The last node points to the first node in a circular linked list.

chapters.title: Stack
chapters.description: Understanding stack data structure and its operations using C++

pages.title: Introduction to Stack
pages.content: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In First Out) principle. The last element inserted into the stack is the first element to be removed.
keyPoints: Deletion also happens from the top

quiz.question: What principle does a stack follow?
quiz.explanation: Stack follows Last In First Out (LIFO) principle.

pages.title: Stack Operations
pages.content: The main operations in a stack are push, pop, and peek. Push inserts an element into the stack, pop removes the top element, and peek returns the top element without removing it.

quiz.question: Which operation removes an element from the stack?
quiz.explanation: Pop removes the top element from the stack.

pages.title: Stack Using Arrays
pages.content: Stacks can be implemented using arrays. The array stores elements while a variable called top keeps track of the current top position.

quiz.question: What variable tracks the top element of a stack?
quiz.explanation: The top variable stores the position of the stack's top element.

pages.title: Stack Using Linked List
pages.content: Stacks can also be implemented using linked lists. This approach avoids the fixed size limitation of arrays.
keyPoints: Push and pop operate at head

quiz.question: What is an advantage of using linked lists for stacks?
quiz.explanation: Linked lists allow dynamic memory allocation for stacks.

pages.title: Stack Overflow and Underflow
pages.content: Stack overflow occurs when trying to push an element into a full stack. Stack underflow occurs when trying to pop an element from an empty stack.
keyPoints: Overflow happens when stack is full
Underflow happens when stack is empty

quiz.question: What happens when pushing into a full stack?
quiz.explanation: Stack overflow occurs when pushing into a full stack.

pages.title: Applications of Stack
pages.content: Stacks are widely used in applications like expression evaluation, syntax parsing, backtracking algorithms, and managing function calls in recursion.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: checking balanced parentheses
keyPoints: Used in recursion and function calls

quiz.question: Where are stacks commonly used?
quiz.explanation: Stacks are used in many algorithmic applications.

chapters.title: Queue
chapters.description: Understanding the queue data structure and its operations using C++

pages.title: Introduction to Queue
pages.content: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the FIFO (First In First Out) principle. The element inserted first is the first one to be removed.

quiz.question: What principle does a queue follow?
quiz.explanation: Queue follows the First In First Out principle.

pages.title: Queue Operations
pages.content: The main operations of a queue are enqueue, dequeue, and peek. Enqueue adds an element to the rear of the queue, dequeue removes an element from the front, and peek returns the front element.

quiz.question: Which operation inserts an element into the queue?
quiz.explanation: Enqueue inserts an element at the rear of the queue.

pages.title: Queue Using Arrays
pages.content: Queues can be implemented using arrays where the front variable tracks the first element and the rear variable tracks the last element.

quiz.question: Which variable tracks the first element in a queue?
quiz.explanation: The front variable points to the first element of the queue.

pages.title: Circular Queue
pages.content: A circular queue improves the efficiency of the simple queue by connecting the end of the queue back to the front. This prevents unused memory spaces.
pages.exampleCode: rear = (rear + 1) % MAX;

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of a circular queue?
quiz.explanation: Circular queues avoid memory wastage in array-based queues.

pages.title: Queue Using Linked List
pages.content: Queues can also be implemented using linked lists. This approach allows dynamic memory allocation and removes the fixed size limitation.

quiz.question: What is an advantage of using linked lists for queues?
quiz.explanation: Linked lists allow dynamic memory allocation.

pages.title: Applications of Queue
pages.content: Queues are used in many real-world applications such as CPU scheduling, printer queues, network data buffering, and Breadth First Search (BFS) algorithms.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: BFS algorithm uses queue

quiz.question: Which graph algorithm uses a queue?
quiz.explanation: Breadth First Search uses a queue.

chapters.title: Trees
chapters.description: Understanding tree data structures and binary trees in Data Structures using C++

pages.title: Introduction to Trees
pages.content: A tree is a hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges. It is widely used to represent hierarchical relationships such as file systems and organizational structures.
keyPoints: Widely used in databases and file systems

quiz.question: What is the top node of a tree called?
quiz.explanation: The topmost node of a tree is called the root.

pages.title: Binary Tree
pages.content: A binary tree is a type of tree data structure where each node has at most two children called the left child and right child.
keyPoints: Each node has at most two children
Children are called left and right

quiz.question: How many children can a binary tree node have?
quiz.explanation: Binary tree nodes can have a maximum of two children.

pages.title: Binary Search Tree (BST)
pages.content: A Binary Search Tree is a special type of binary tree where the left child contains smaller values and the right child contains larger values compared to the parent node.

quiz.question: Where are smaller values stored in a Binary Search Tree?
quiz.explanation: In BST, smaller values are stored in the left subtree.

pages.title: Tree Traversals
pages.content: Tree traversal means visiting all nodes in a tree in a specific order. Common traversal methods include Inorder, Preorder, and Postorder.
keyPoints: Common traversals are inorder, preorder, postorder

quiz.question: Which traversal visits left subtree, root, then right subtree?
quiz.explanation: Inorder traversal visits left subtree, root, then right subtree.

pages.title: Preorder and Postorder Traversal
pages.content: Preorder traversal visits the root first, then the left subtree, and finally the right subtree. Postorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, and finally the root.

quiz.question: Which traversal visits the root node first?
quiz.explanation: Preorder traversal visits the root node first.

pages.title: Applications of Trees
pages.content: Trees are widely used in many applications such as databases, file systems, network routing algorithms, and expression evaluation.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: File system structure uses trees

quiz.question: Where are tree data structures commonly used?
quiz.explanation: Trees are used in many real-world systems.

chapters.title: Graphs
chapters.description: Understanding graph data structures and traversal algorithms used in Data Structures

pages.title: Introduction to Graphs
pages.content: A graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Graphs are used to represent relationships between objects such as networks and maps.
keyPoints: Graph consists of vertices and edges

quiz.question: What are the basic components of a graph?
quiz.explanation: Graphs consist of vertices (nodes) and edges.

pages.title: Types of Graphs
pages.content: Graphs can be categorized into different types such as directed graphs, undirected graphs, weighted graphs, and unweighted graphs depending on how edges connect vertices.
keyPoints: Weighted graphs assign values to edges

quiz.question: Which graph type has edges with direction?
quiz.explanation: Directed graphs have edges with specific direction.

pages.title: Graph Representation
pages.content: Graphs can be represented using two main methods: adjacency matrix and adjacency list. These representations help store graph data efficiently in memory.
keyPoints: Adjacency list uses linked lists or vectors
List is more efficient for sparse graphs

quiz.question: Which representation uses a 2D array?
quiz.explanation: Adjacency matrix uses a 2D array.

pages.title: Breadth First Search (BFS)
pages.content: Breadth First Search is a graph traversal algorithm that explores all neighbors of a node before moving to the next level. It uses a queue data structure.

quiz.question: Which data structure is used in BFS?
quiz.explanation: BFS uses a queue to manage nodes.

pages.title: Depth First Search (DFS)
pages.content: Depth First Search explores as far as possible along a branch before backtracking. It is commonly implemented using recursion or a stack.

quiz.question: Which data structure is commonly used in DFS?
quiz.explanation: DFS uses a stack or recursion.

pages.title: Applications of Graphs
pages.content: Graphs are widely used in real-world applications such as social networks, navigation systems, recommendation systems, and network routing algorithms.
pages.exampleCode: // Example: Google Maps uses graph algorithms

quiz.question: Where are graph algorithms commonly used?
quiz.explanation: Graph algorithms are used in many real-world applications.

chapters.title: Hashing
chapters.description: Understanding hashing techniques and hash tables used for fast data retrieval

pages.title: Introduction to Hashing
pages.content: Hashing is a technique used to map data to a fixed-size table using a hash function. It allows very fast data retrieval, usually in constant time.
pages.exampleCode:
// Example concept
key -> hashFunction(key) -> index

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of hashing?
quiz.explanation: Hashing is used for fast data retrieval.

pages.title: Hash Table
pages.content: A hash table is a data structure that stores key-value pairs. It uses a hash function to determine the index where a value should be stored.
keyPoints: Uses hash function to find index

quiz.question: What does a hash table store?
quiz.explanation: Hash tables store key-value pairs.

pages.title: Hash Function
pages.content: A hash function converts a key into an index in the hash table. A good hash function distributes keys evenly across the table.

quiz.question: What does a hash function return?
quiz.explanation: A hash function returns an index for storing data.

pages.title: Collision in Hashing
pages.content: A collision occurs when two keys generate the same hash index. Collisions must be handled properly to maintain performance.
keyPoints: Collision occurs when two keys share same index

quiz.question: What is a collision in hashing?
quiz.explanation: Collision occurs when two keys produce the same index.

pages.title: Collision Handling Techniques

interviewQuestions.question: What is a Data Structure?
interviewQuestions.answer: A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
interviewQuestions.answer: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory locations and allow direct access by index, while linked lists store elements in nodes connected by pointers and do not require contiguous memory.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a stack?
interviewQuestions.answer: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last In First Out) principle where the last element added is the first one removed.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a queue?
interviewQuestions.answer: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the FIFO (First In First Out) principle where the first element added is the first one removed.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an array?
interviewQuestions.answer: The time complexity is O(1) because array elements can be accessed directly using an index.

interviewQuestions.question: What is recursion?
interviewQuestions.answer: Recursion is a technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of a problem until a base condition is reached.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a binary tree?
interviewQuestions.answer: A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children called the left child and right child.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
interviewQuestions.answer: A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree where the left subtree contains smaller values and the right subtree contains larger values than the root node.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
interviewQuestions.answer: BFS (Breadth First Search) explores nodes level by level using a queue, while DFS (Depth First Search) explores as far as possible along a branch before backtracking using a stack or recursion.

interviewQuestions.question: What is hashing?
interviewQuestions.answer: Hashing is a technique used to map keys to specific indexes in a hash table using a hash function for fast data retrieval.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a hash table?
interviewQuestions.answer: A hash table is a data structure that stores key-value pairs and uses a hash function to compute the index where the data is stored.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a collision in hashing?
interviewQuestions.answer: A collision occurs when two different keys produce the same hash value and map to the same index in a hash table.

interviewQuestions.question: What are the ways to resolve collisions in hashing?
interviewQuestions.answer: Common collision resolution techniques include chaining and open addressing methods such as linear probing and quadratic probing.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
interviewQuestions.answer: The time complexity of binary search is O(log n) because the search space is halved at each step.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a heap?
interviewQuestions.answer: A heap is a complete binary tree where the parent node is either greater than (max heap) or smaller than (min heap) its children.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a priority queue?
interviewQuestions.answer: A priority queue is a data structure where elements are served based on priority rather than insertion order.

interviewQuestions.question: What is dynamic programming?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dynamic programming is an optimization technique that solves complex problems by breaking them into smaller overlapping subproblems and storing results for reuse.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between greedy algorithms and dynamic programming?
interviewQuestions.answer: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step, while dynamic programming considers all possibilities and stores intermediate results.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a graph?
interviewQuestions.answer: A graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of vertices connected by edges used to represent relationships between objects.

interviewQuestions.question: What is topological sorting?
interviewQuestions.answer: Topological sorting is a linear ordering of vertices in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u → v, vertex u appears before v.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Dijkstra's algorithm?
interviewQuestions.answer: Dijkstra's algorithm is used to find the shortest path from a source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a tree and a graph?
interviewQuestions.answer: A tree is a special type of graph that has no cycles and is connected, while a graph may contain cycles and may or may not be connected.

interviewQuestions.question: What is a minimum spanning tree?
interviewQuestions.answer: A minimum spanning tree is a subset of edges in a weighted graph that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Kruskal's algorithm?
interviewQuestions.answer: Kruskal's algorithm finds the minimum spanning tree by selecting the smallest edges while avoiding cycles.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Prim's algorithm?
interviewQuestions.answer: Prim's algorithm finds the minimum spanning tree by starting from a vertex and repeatedly adding the smallest edge that connects a new vertex.

interviewQuestions.question: What is backtracking?
interviewQuestions.answer: Backtracking is an algorithmic technique that tries different possibilities and backtracks when a solution path fails.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between linear search and binary search?
interviewQuestions.answer: Linear search checks each element sequentially while binary search repeatedly divides the sorted array in half to locate the target.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Kadane's Algorithm?
interviewQuestions.answer: Kadane's Algorithm is used to find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray in linear time.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the sliding window technique?
interviewQuestions.answer: The sliding window technique is used to reduce time complexity when working with subarrays by maintaining a window that moves across the array.

interviewQuestions.question: What is memoization?
interviewQuestions.answer: Memoization is an optimization technique used in dynamic programming where results of expensive function calls are stored and reused.
